source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 78a 'Timbo Limbo' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Overworked Lydia, sent alone with a jug heavier than herself, is heard crying at the river by a Jack-fish, Timbo Limbo, who offers to help if she will be his wife; their song summons him each morning. The spying half-sibling betrays the secret, the father calls the fish out with the stolen song and shoots him, and a single scale flies two miles to fall on Lydia's breast. Learning the truth, she sings three times at the river — the water turns blood — and drowns herself where her husband's body was not.
summary.zh: 重役之下的莉迪亞獨負巨壺至河邊啜泣； Jack 魚廷波林波聞聲相助，許以婚約，並以歌相召。同父異母的妹妹窺探告密，父親用偷學的歌聲喚魚出水槍殺之；一片魚鱗飛行兩哩落在莉迪亞胸前。她知情後三次臨河而歌——河水化血——最後在丈夫不在的水中投河自盡。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale (fish-husband/animal-bridegroom type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A man had one daughter named Lydia. His wife died and he married another woman, who had children for the man and liked her own children more than the daughter-in-law — mostly it was the daughter-in-law she imposed the work on. She sent Lydia for water, giving her a big jug heavier than Lydia's weight, and would not send any of her own children to help Lydia up. When Lydia got to the river-side she was crying that the jug was too heavy and she could get no one to help her up; a Jack-fish in the river heard the lament, came up, and said that if she would be a wife to him he would help her up whenever she came to the river-side. Lydia consented, filled her jar, and the Jack-fish helped her up and she went to the yard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother-in-law pressed her about who had helped her up with the jar, and Lydia said she had no one. One morning she took up the jug and went to the river-side — the mother-in-law had sent one of her children to follow and watch who helped her up. Lydia had to sing to call the Jack-fish, whose name was Timbo Limbo: 'Timbo Limbo, same gal Lydia, Timbo Limbo o-o-o!' — and when the fish heard the voice of Lydia he came up to help her. The little child saw the Jack-fish, went home, and told her mother: 'Mamma, me sister Lydia does have a man-fish at the river-side to help her up.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78a, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: At night the man was told; at daylight he had Lydia dressed and sent on to Montego Bay to buy pepper and skelion. He loaded his gun and went with the little girl to the river-side; the little girl sang the song three times, changing her voice, and the water went round so, and the Jack-fish came out — the father shot him. He stripped, jumped in, swam, took out the Jack-fish and carried him to the yard. As he began to scale the fish, one of the scales flew all the way, some two miles, and met Lydia and dropped at her breast; when she took it off she found it was a Timbo Limbo scale. She started crying, ran to the yard, took up her jar, went to the river and started her song — the Jack-fish didn't come up; she sang again, the water stayed steady; she sang again, the water turned blood. And when she found that Timbo Limbo was not in the water, Lydia took herself up and drowned herself right in the water. Jack man dory, choose none!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 78b 'Fish fish fish' (told by Florence Thomlinson, Lacovia)

summary.en: One daughter goes to the river-side to worship a little fish with her song; the other daughter, sent instead the next day, copies the tune, catches the fish, and the family cooks it — saving a plate for the true friend, who refuses it and sings until all the fish rise and turn into one big fish she carries back to the river.
summary.zh: 一個女兒到河邊以歌敬奉小魚；次日被派去的另一個女兒照抄歌調，把魚捕回家烹食——還特意留一份給真正的朋友。她不吃，只是一路唱下去，直到所有的魚浮起、化為一條大魚，她把它捧回河中。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale; 'worship' of a fish is folkloric devotion within a tale, not ritual instruction. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: It was a mother and two daughters. One of the daughters went to the river-side to worship a little fish; she commenced to sing — 'Fish, fish, fish, fish, pengeleng; come on the river, pengeleng' — and the little fish came to her. She played, played, played, let go the fish, and the fish went back into the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she went back home her mother quarreled that she had waited back so long; the next day she would not send her back to the river but sent the other daughter, who sang the same song she had heard her sister sing. She caught the fish and brought it home; they cooked the fish for dinner and saved some for the other daughter. When she came she would not eat it, for she knew it was the said fish; she began to sing 'Fish fish fish fish, pengeleng!' — and the other sister said, 'Tank God, me no eat de fish!' The mother said, 'Tank God, me no eat de fish!' She went on singing until all the fish came up and turned into one big fish, and she took it and put it back in the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78b, ending (1924); not verbatim.

region.zh: 牙買加聖安克萊爾蒙特

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 78c 'Dear Old Juna' (told by Richard Pottinger, Claremont, St. Ann)

summary.en: A girl betrothed to both a man and a fish cooks breakfast for each at ten o'clock, carrying a waiter of food to the river and singing Juna up: 'You mother run, you father forsake you, you don't know you deh!' — 'Kai, kai, Juna, me know you!' The jealous lover borrows the song, shoots the fish at breakfast, dresses and serves it, and everyone eats — until the girl finds out whose body it was, and drops dead at the instant.
summary.zh: 同時許身於人與魚的姑娘，每天十點為兩位『未婚夫』各備早飯，托盤送至河邊，唱喚茹娜出水——『你母親跑了，你父親棄了你，你還不知道自己在此！』——『嗨，嗨，茹娜，我認得你！』妒火中燒的未婚夫借得歌調，在早餐時一槍斃魚，烹而饗客——待姑娘認出盤中是誰，當場倒斃。

sensitivity.note: Animal-bridegroom tragedy type. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A man and a woman had but one daughter who was their pet. The girl was engaged to a fish, and to another young man too; generally at ten o'clock she cooked breakfast for the both. The man at home ate; then she took a waiter with the fish's breakfast to the river. When she went to the river she had to sing a song that the fish might come out: 'Dear old Juna, dear old Juna, oona a da vina sa... You mother run, you father forsake you, you don't know you deh!' Fish came now, singing, 'Kai, kai, Juna, me know you!' — and the fish came out to have his breakfast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78c (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: It went on for several days, every day she sang the same and the fish gave the same reply. The young man thought of it now; one morning he went a little earlier with his gun, singing the same tune. The fish came out and sang the same tune as it generally did; the young man shot it, carried the fish home, dressed it, and everybody ate now — the gal and everybody. At the end of the eating she found out it was the said fish, and she dropped dead at the instant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78c, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Juggin Straw Blue and the Seven-Headed Witch
title.zh: 賈金·斯特勞·布魯與七頭巫師

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 79 'Juggin Straw Blue' (told by David Roach, Lacovia)

summary.en: Helped with her water-tub by an Old Witch man and sworn to secrecy, the niece betrays her helper; the aunt locks her in an iron chest, but tears through the keyhole are licked up — 'after the fat is so sweet, what says the flesh!' — and the witch bursts the door. Marching her off with music in his knock-knees, he sings his menu — your head and lights for my dog, your liver for my supper — until her sweetheart's mother issues eight eggs against the witch's seven heads and seven eggs; an egg smashed buys a day of light and a head cut off, until the last head falls and the girl goes home to be married.
summary.zh: 女孩受老巫相助卻泄密；姨母把她鎖進鐵箱，淚水卻從鎖孔滴出被巫舔盡——『脂膏如此香甜，血肉又當如何！』——箱門迸裂。巫以膝響為樂，唱著菜單押行——頭與心肝喂狗、肝臟為晚餐——直到戀人之母授八枚雞蛋以破七頭七蛋之局：碎一蛋換一日天光、斫一首級；第七顆頭落地，女孩得救歸嫁。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale (seven-headed ogre/egg-and-head duel type, ATU 302-linked). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A woman had a daughter and a niece, and the niece was courting one Juggin Straw Blue. The aunt loved the daughter more and always wanted the niece to do more work. One day she sent the niece to the river with a big tub; the girl filled it and could not lift it. An Old Witch man was by the river-side; he helped her up and told her not to tell anybody who helped her. But when she went home the aunt pumped her until she told; the aunt knew the Old Witch man would come for her in the night, and locked her in an iron chest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 79 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Part of the night the Old Witch man came in search of the girl. She was crying in the iron chest, and the tears went through the keyhole; he wiped it and licked it and said, 'After the fat is so sweet, what says the flesh!' And he burst the door open and took her out. He traveled with the girl, knock-kneed, the sound of his knee like music; and he said to her, 'Your head and your lights are for my dog, and your liver is for my supper!' So the girl started a song — 'Why, why, why, my Juggin Straw Blue... this rotten stuff, this stinking stuff, then carry me down to gully True Blue, you'll see me no more.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 79, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: As the girl was courting Juggin Straw Blue, his mother was an Old Witch too. The courting boy's mother waked him up and gave him eight eggs — for the Old Witch man had seven heads and seven eggs, one egg for each head. The boy went after the Old Witch man and overtook him and mashed one of the eggs — and daylight came — and he cut off one of the heads. The Old Witch man mashed one of his eggs and night came back; the boy mashed the next one and daylight again; and so they went on, the boy mashing seven eggs and cutting off the Old Witch's seven heads, taking away his girl — and he went home with his girl and married.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 79, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Witch and the Grain of Peas

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 80 'The Witch and the Grain of Peas' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: The witch mother-in-law counts her boiling peas grain by grain, finds one missing, and swears the thieving daughter-in-law at the river: eat my peas today and you will be drowned. The girl's death-song reaches her sweetheart William, who gathers four limes, four hen's eggs, four turkey's eggs and four marbles, meets the witch in battle at the river-side, kills her, and carries the girl home to marry.
summary.zh: 巫婆岳母逐粒清點鍋中豌豆，發現少了一粒，便押繼女到河邊發誓：今日吃我一粒豌豆，便溺斃於此。女孩的哀歌傳到戀人威廉耳中；他備齊四枚青檸、四枚雞蛋、四枚火雞蛋與四顆彈珠，在河邊與巫婆決戰，殺之，攜女歸家成婚。

sensitivity.note: Witch-execution wonder tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A man was first married to a woman and had one child with her. She died and he married another, and the girl had to call her mother-in-law — who did not like the daughter-in-law, who lived in a house by herself. One day the mother-in-law washed some peas, put them on the fire, and went away to her ground; the daughter-in-law came to the house to catch the daughter, louse and comb her hair. The mother-in-law, an Old Witch, knew the daughter-in-law had come to the house; the daughter said, 'Look here, sister, mamma put some peas on the fire — why don't you take one grain of the peas?' And she opened the pot and took out one grain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 80 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Old Witch woman knew the daughter-in-law had taken out one grain, she put up her hoe, came back from the ground, took down the pot, turned out all the peas in a bowl, and coupled every grain until she found one that had no match. 'Look here! Did your sister come today?' — 'No, never came today!' — 'Yes, don't control me, for I see at the grain that your sister came and took out one grain from the pot.' She swore her at the river to drown her because she took the peas: 'If you don't eat my peas today you won't be drowned, but if you eat my peas you will be drowned.' So the girl took up her song — 'Oh, me dearest mama, me mama... a ring down, peace, oh, a ring down...'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 80, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the said time the young girl had a sweetheart outside named William. William's mother heard the song on the river-side and sent word to the carpenter-shop that William's girl was singing quite mournful there. He went up a lime-tree and picked four limes, went to a fowl-nest and took four fowl-eggs, went to a turkey-nest and took four turkey-eggs, took four marbles, called the girl and put her before him; and William and the girl's mother-in-law came to a battle at the river-side, and William killed the woman. He put the girl before him, carried her home and married her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 80, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 81 'Bosen Corner' (told by Martha Roe, Maroon Town)

summary.en: On the road to Old Witch country the kind daughter-in-law greets the so-so head and crossed feet, is fed from one bone and four grains of rice, scratches the witch's back to blood without a word, and hugs the old cat sent in her place. Told to take the little eggs that cry 'don't take me' and break one at each of four crossroads, she finds a common, a drove of stock, a gentleman in a buggy, and a prince who marries her. The greedy own daughter, sent the same road, mocks the bugaboos, flings out the cat, and smashes the big eggs that cry 'take me' — snakes, insects, and a tearing Old Witch man kill her in the road.
summary.zh: 善良的媳婦一路向『孤頭』『交叉腳』問好，吃一骨四米之宴，為巫婆抓背抓到流血而不言，還抱起替代老嫗的老貓。聽囑取那喊『別拿我』的小蛋，在四個十字路口逐一打破——得一片牧場、一群牛羊、一位馬車紳士、一位提親王子。貪心的親生女走同一條路，譏笑鬼怪、摔貓出門、專取喊『拿我』的大蛋——蛇、蟲與撕裂人的老巫把她在路中殺死。

sensitivity.note: Two-sisters witch-road tale (Frau Holle type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A woman had two daughters: one her own child, one her daughter-in-law, whom she did not use well. The place where they went for water was a bad place, Old Witch country, called Bosen Corner. One day she sent the daughter-in-law for water. Going along, she saw a so-so (only) head in the road and put her hand on her belly to make a kind howdy. Further on she saw two feet crossed in the road — 'Howdy, papa.' — 'Gal, where you going?' — 'Mamma sent me to Bosen Corner for water.' — 'Go on, gal; good before and bad behind.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 81 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: She went on to a little hut where one old lady sat — 'Come in here; late night going to take you.' The Old Witch picked up a piece of bone from the dung-heap, chopped it up in the pot with four grains of rice, and boiled the pot full of meat and rice for the girl's dinner. When she had eaten, the old lady called her to scratch her back; as the girl's hand scratched, the back picked all the skin off her hand till it bled — 'What is the matter with your hand?' — 'Nothing, ma'am.' When she sat down, the old lady went out of the door and came in an old cat, which the girl hugged up and coaxed and was so kind to; then she slept and got up to go away in the morning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 81, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old lady told her to go round the house and see some fowl-eggs: the eggs that cry 'Take me! take me!' are big eggs, she must not take them; the small eggs that say 'Don't take me!' she must take four. At the first crossroad she mashed one and saw into a big pretty common; at the second, the common packed up with cows, goats, sheep and everything a gentleman possesses; at the third, a pretty young gentleman came out into a buggy; at the fourth she mashed the last egg and found the gentleman was a prince, and he married her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 81, middle-b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The daughter-in-law came with her husband and drove into the yard, and the mother-in-law, expecting the Old Witch had killed the girl, sent her own daughter to Bosen Corner for water too. The girl mocked as she went — 'Ay-e-e! from me born I never see so-so head yet!' — was told 'Go long, gal! better day before,' ate the same bone-and-rice dinner, turned a puss and flung the begging cat out the door, had her hands cut scratching, and in the morning took four of the big eggs. First crossroad: a whole heap of snakes; second: a whole lot of insects; at the last crossroad she mashed one and saw a big Old Witch man, who tore her up and killed her stiff dead in the road.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 81, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Three Dogs: Blum-blum, Sinde, Dido
title.zh: 三犬記：布倫布倫、辛德、狄多

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 82a 'Boy and Witch Woman' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Begging fire from the Old Witch's kitchen, the witch-born William watches her knock children out of her own skin and beats her test — 'Boy, you just as good as me!' — by catching fire in rotten wood without her fire-stick. Marked for revenge, he wins the packey-knock courtship, is nearly razor-murdered in the night by his grumbling dogs Blum-blum, Sinde and Dido, leaves a boiling-blood basin as alarm with his deaf mother, and is stranded atop an apple-tree while the witch knocks out forty axe-men to fell it — until the basin boils over, the chained dogs come flying, and destroy the axe-men and the witch, whose scattered pieces are the cowitch weed of the whole earth.
summary.zh: 向老巫廚房討火時，巫種出身的威廉窺見她敲皮出子，又以朽木引火不取其火棒——『你這孩子，不比我差！』被記仇的巫以擲罐選婿之局選中；夜裡剃刀臨頸，三犬布倫布倫、辛德、狄多低吠破局。他留下沸血之盆為警報託付聾母；被誘上蘋果樹時，巫喚出四十斧手伐樹——盆血沸溢，鎖鏈掙斷，三犬騰空而至，誅斧手與老巫；撒遍大地的巫屍碎片，便是如今的毒漆草。

sensitivity.note: Witch-slayer wonder tale (animal-helper cycle, ATU 325-302-linked). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Olden time it was a young man and his brother, bred up on a property penning cows. Every morning they wanted to pen, carrying their breakfast and their fire; one morning the food came but no fire. At twelve o'clock the smaller brother felt hungry and went to look for fire up a hillside where a smoke showed, and found a big open house, a lady in the open kitchen — an Old Witch. He was frightened and came back; then the bigger brother, William, went. He stopped behind a big dry stump and watched what the Old Witch did: she took a pot off the fire and dished out all the vessels right through, though no pickney was in the kitchen — only the Old Witch. She knocked on her side, pon-pon-pon, and all the children came out, twenty big men and small children, women and boy pickney; they sat and ate, smoked, and then she knocked again and all the children went up into her back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy called, 'Mawnin', Nana!' She was frightened, asked if he had been there long; he said he had only come up to beg for fire. 'Take fire, but don't take my fire-stick!' — and the boy turned back, broke a piece of rotten wood, held it against the steam of the fire and caught it alight. The Old Witch said, 'Boy, you just as good as me!' — 'No, Nana, I'm not so good!' William went down to the cow-pen, told his smaller brother not to make up fire but to pen the cows and go home quick quick — for this bigger brother was a witch himself and knew all about what would come after him; he went inside the house and fawned sick. In quick time the Old Witch was upon them, and said anyone who could knock the packey off her head she would take for a husband; the smaller brother flung and failed, and William, coming out sick, picked up a little trash and knocked it off — 'Yes, you is my husband!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82a, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the night, when William was in dead sleep, the Old Witch took a razor to cut his throat. William had three dogs — Blum-blum, Shade, and Dido — and when she took the razor, Blum-blum grumbled and the razor's mouth turned over; William woke. Twice more she rose, singing 'Sharpen me razor, sharpen me razor' — Sinde grumbled, then Dido grumbled, and the razor's mouth turned over. At daylight William and his wife went away into witch country, leaving a big white basin in the hall middle: as soon as it boiled up in blood, his mother must let go the three dogs. On the road the witch flung a marble to an apple-tree and begged William kindly to climb and pick the apple — 'Hah! I tell you I got you today! The place where you see me knock out pickney out of my skin, you will have to tell me today.' — 'Yes, I know about that long time, for it will be iron cut iron today!' — and the witch knocked out ten axe-men to fell the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82a, middle-b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: William started his song — 'Blum-blum, Sinde, Dido...' — and the Old Witch sang hers — 'Chin, fallah, fallah...' When the tree was going to fall William said, 'Bear me up, me good tree! Many time me fader fell a green tree, leave a dry one.' The witch knocked out twenty axe-men, thirty axe-men; while William was in the tree, the white basin boiled up with blood, and his deaf mother, chattering with a neighbor all day, saw the blood stream slap on her frock, cut the chain of Blum-blum and Sinde — Dido cut his chain himself — and the three dogs galloped away. William, up the tree, only shook his hand, and the three dogs dropped; they waited until the Old Witch had forty axe-men round the tree, and in the height of the cutting destroyed every one of them and killed the Old Witch herself. William came down, took his machete and scattered the Old Witch over the whole earth — everywhere you go, that bad cowitch is nothing else than the pieces of the Old Witch. Jack man dory, choose now!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Lucy and Janet: Manners against the Witch

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 82b 'Lucy and Janet' (told by Martha Roe, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: Kind Lucy eats her school-road breakfast with the three escort dogs as with friends, and when the Old Witch man springs out to destroy her, the dogs run in and tear him up. Rude Janet, who quarrels at the escort's lateness and eats first before dividing the leftovers, calls the dogs harshly in her turn — and they will not come; the Old Witch kills the girl through her bad manners. 'Money won't take you round the island like civility.'
summary.zh: 溫良的露西與護送的三犬同桌共食如友；老巫竄出欲害她時，三犬撲上撕裂了他。粗魯的珍奈先責護送來遲，吃罷才分剩食，呼犬時聲色俱厲——犬不應命；老巫便因她的無禮殺了她。『錢財帶不動你環島，禮貌才行。』

sensitivity.note: Moral animal-helper tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Once a woman had two daughters, Lucy and Janet, sent far to school. There was an Old Witch living along the road, and she had three dogs — Dick, Dandy, and Bellamo. In August, Lucy was going home to spend time with her mamma, and the mother had to send the three dogs to carry her home, all her breakfast for her and the dogs put together. Lucy was kind; when she came to her breakfast, she and the three dogs ate together, never considering them as dogs but as friends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82b (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she came halfway, the three dogs stopped back and one big Old Witch man came out to destroy Lucy; the dogs had left her quite behind, and she called them: 'Yah! Bellamo, Dick and Dandy, yah! Bellamo, yo!' The three dogs ran in and tore up the Old Witch and killed him. Every time Lucy came, the three dogs guided her to her mamma to spend August, and carried her back to her school-missus's place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82b, middle (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Christmas Janet went. The dogs came to carry her home, and when they came she said, 'I wonder what you all doing so long!' and began to quarrel; when she got to eat breakfast, she ate her breakfast first, then divided what was left to give the dogs. As she started on, the dogs fell back the same as usual; when the Old Witch man came out, she called the dogs harshly — and the dogs would not come. The Old Witch killed that girl through her bad manners. So you find plenty of young people who don't have manners: money won't take you round the island like civility.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82b, ending (2024/1924); not verbatim.
